# Writing a claim producer with the typed-data mix-in

A claim producer that also implements the data-processing protocol gets staged
candidates per fan-out partition, committed together on success and collected on
failure, plus a version history readers reach through rimsky's own routes.

## Prove the protocol before wiring it up

Both suites ship in the CLI and need only your producer running.

```bash
rimsky conformance data-processing --endpoint grpc://127.0.0.1:9700
rimsky conformance claim-producer  --endpoint grpc://127.0.0.1:9700
```

The data-processing suite runs ten checks: capabilities, begin-then-commit per
materialization, begin idempotency, the three abandon checks, the list-versions,
list-partitions and get-version-schema smokes, and concurrent writes.

## Declare both protocols on one entry

```yaml
persistence:
  driver: sqlite
  sqlite:
    path: /var/lib/rimsky/state.db
claim_producers:
  typed:
    endpoint: "producer:9700"
    protocols: ["claim_producer", "data_processing"]
    write_semantics_allowed: ["staged_async"]
named_locks: {}
executors:
  "typed-exec":
    transport: grpc
    endpoint: "producer:9700"
    protocols: ["executor"]
```

```bash
curl -sS "$BASE/v1/observability/claim-producers/typed"
# reachability_status: reachable
```

## Stage one candidate per partition

```yaml
name: dataproc
version: "1"
nodes:
  - type: good
    executor: typed-exec
    claim_producers:
      - name: typed
        selector: dataset-good
        intent: rw
        alias: root
        lifetime: durable
    error_types:
      "acquire/unavailable": {action: retry}
    fan_out:
      claim: root
      partition_request: '{"parts":3}'
      error_policy:
        kind: best_effort
    attributes:
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          outcome: {type: string, default: ok}
          echo:    {type: string, default: good}

  - type: bad
    executor: typed-exec
    claim_producers:
      - name: typed
        selector: dataset-bad
        intent: rw
        alias: root
        lifetime: durable
    error_types:
      "acquire/unavailable": {action: retry}
    fan_out:
      claim: root
      partition_request: '{"parts":2}'
      error_policy:
        kind: best_effort
    attributes:
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          outcome: {type: string, default: fail}
          echo:    {type: string, default: bad}
```

## What the product does

Rimsky calls `SplitScope` once per fan-out node, then opens one staging
candidate per partition — five `BeginCandidate` calls across the three-way and
two-way splits — keyed by the partition names the producer itself returned.

When a fan-out's children settle, its candidates are committed: three
`CommitCandidate` calls for the successful fan-out. When a fan-out's children
error, its candidates are abandoned: two `AbandonCandidate` calls for the
failing one.

Nothing is left staged either way, and exactly three versions exist afterwards,
one per committed partition, keyed `part-0`, `part-1`, `part-2`.

A reader of your store sees a partition's data only once that partition is
complete, and a failed write leaves nothing behind to clean up.

## Version history reaches readers through your own listing surface

The fan-out's claim appears as an asset:

```bash
curl -sS "$BASE/v1/instances/$IID/assets"
curl -sS "$BASE/v1/instances/$IID/assets/$ALIAS/versions"

rimsky asset versions --instance "$IID" "$ALIAS" -o json --endpoint "$BASE"
```

Both paths call your producer's own `ListVersions` verb. What a reader gets back
is whatever your data model holds, surfaced through rimsky rather than replaced
by it: you own the version history and rimsky owns the route to it.

If your producer records versions against sub-claim handles rather than against
the parent handle the asset route names, the asset's version listing comes back
empty. That is your data model's choice, not the route's.
